# Desktop apps

> **PocketBase:** a server you host, reached from a browser. **PocketOne:** the same app folder also builds into a native desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, with your hooks, migrations and pages inside one executable and each user's data on their own machine.

Your app is a folder: `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations` and `pb_public`. `pocketone serve` runs it as a server, as always.
`pocketone desktop build` turns the same folder into an app your users double-click:

```sh
pocketone serve                  # the app as a server
pocketone desktop build          # a desktop app for this machine, in dist/
pocketone desktop build --all    # macOS, Windows and Linux, arm64 and amd64
```

All you need is `pocketone` and Docker. The build runs in a build image that holds Go and PocketOne's source, so
there's no Go, C compiler or Xcode to install, and every platform builds from any machine.

> **Preview.** Desktop builds work today, but how a desktop app handles trust and settings is still settling (see
> [What's next](#whats-next)). The desktop runtime uses Wails' cgo-free backends, which Wails marks experimental on
> macOS and Linux.

## How it works

The desktop app is your PocketOne app plus a window:

1. Your `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations` and `pb_public` are embedded in the executable. Nothing is read from disk, so
   nobody can change a shipped app's hooks.
2. When it starts, it runs your app's server on a private `127.0.0.1` port, applying your migrations to the user's data.
3. It opens a native window on that server, using the system's own webview: WebKit on macOS, WebView2 on Windows,
   WebKitGTK on Linux.

Your pages call the API with `fetch`, exactly as they do in a browser. The PocketBase JS SDK, realtime and file
uploads work the same, because it's the same server.

## Try it: hello world

PocketOne's source has a hello-world app in `ext/desktop/example/hello`: a hook, a migration and one page that lists
and adds greetings.

```js
// pb_hooks/main.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/api/hello", (e) => {
  const rows = $app.findRecordsByFilter("greetings", "", "-created", 50, 0)
  return e.json(200, { message: "Hello from PocketOne hooks", greetings: rows.map((r) => r.get("text")) })
})
```

Its `pocketone.yaml` keeps the server's data in the folder and names the desktop app:

```yaml
app:
  dir: pb_data
server:
  public_dir: pb_public
desktop:
  name: Hello
  id: dev.pocketone.hello
  width: 900
  height: 640
```

Run it both ways:

```sh
cd ext/desktop/example/hello
pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password
pocketone serve                  # http://127.0.0.1:8090
pocketone desktop build          # dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app on an Apple Silicon Mac
open dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app
```

The server and the desktop app keep separate data: the server's in `pb_data/`, the desktop app's in your app-data
folder.

## What's next

A desktop app has one person at the keyboard and data on their machine, so PocketBase's users and superusers don't
quite fit. Being worked out:

- **Trust:** requests from the app's own window run as its owner, and nothing else on the machine can reach the server.
- **Settings:** a native Preferences window for the settings your app and its extensions declare, since the superuser
  dashboard isn't part of a shipped app.
